q.intro.text: Every real number has a place on this map. Root two, root three and pi sit in Irrational: their decimals never end and never repeat. Add two irrational numbers. Is the sum always irrational, sometimes, or never? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked sometimes, and you were right. Now you can show why: one pair that lands outside is enough.

q.cb.always.text: At the start you picked always. Examples like root two plus root three make it look that way, but root two plus negative root two is zero, and that breaks it.

q.cb.never.text: At the start you picked never. But root two plus root three is irrational. The answer is sometimes.

q.cb.none.text: Irrational numbers are not closed under addition or multiplication. One counterexample each shows it.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the map moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Root two, negative root two and root three are all irrational: none of them is a ratio of integers. They sit in the Irrational region, beside Rational, never inside it.

e.step1.text: Root two plus root three stays irrational. So does root two plus root two. Two pairs that work. But the claim says every pair, and a few examples can never check infinitely many pairs.

e.step2.text: Try opposites. Root two plus negative root two is zero. Both inputs are irrational, and zero lands in Whole, outside Irrational. One pair is enough: the irrationals are not closed under addition. The answer is sometimes.

e.step3.text: The rationals are different. Any two are a over b and c over d, with integers, and b and d not zero. The sum is a d plus b c, over b d: integers over a nonzero integer, for every pair. Rational plus rational is always rational. Closed.

e.why.text: Quick check: why does one pair settle it, when two pairs that worked did not?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. An always claim needs every case. One valid counterexample settles it, however many examples worked.

e.why.exc.text: Both inputs were irrational, so the pair is allowed. A claim about every pair has no exceptions.

e.why.most.text: Mostly is not always. The claim is false: the sum is only sometimes irrational.

t.intro.text: Now multiply two irrational numbers. Is the product always irrational? The first two steps are done for you.

t.pair.text: Which pair could break the claim? Both inputs must be irrational, and the product must land outside Irrational.

t.pair.ok.text: Yes. Both inputs are irrational. Let's see where the product lands.

t.pair.in.text: That one stays inside: root fifteen is irrational. A counterexample has to land outside.

t.pair.zero.text: Zero is rational, not irrational, so the claim says nothing about this pair. Both inputs must be irrational.

t.v.text: What is root three times root three, exactly?

t.v.nine.text: Root three is not three. Root three is the positive number whose square is three. So what is root three times root three?

t.v.approx.text: Close, but use the exact meaning, not a calculator. The square of root three is exactly three.

t.v.no.text: Root three is the number whose square is three. What is root three times root three?

t.v.ok.text: Yes. Exactly three, by the meaning of the square root.

t.sets.text: The product is three. Which list names every set that three belongs to?

t.sets.ok.text: Yes. Three sits in Counting, and every region around it holds it too.

t.sets.only.text: The sets are nested. Three is a counting number, so it is whole, an integer, rational and real too.

t.sets.root.text: Classify by the value. The product is exactly three, wherever it came from.

p.intro.text: Sam says: three plus root two might be rational. Nobody has checked all of its digits. Is Sam right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.no.assume.text: We do not know that. It is only supposed, to see where it leads. The supposition is what gets tested.

p.no.example.text: One value of q proves nothing about every q. The reason is closure: rational minus rational is always rational.

p.no.bar.text: Any number can be written with a fraction bar, like root two over one. Rational means integers over a nonzero integer, and closure gives that here.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.c1.text: Right. An indirect proof starts by supposing the opposite and following it.

p.c2.text: Right. Subtract three from both sides: the three and the minus three are opposites, and they cancel.

p.c3.text: Right. Rational minus rational is always rational: the rationals are closed under subtraction.

p.c4.text: Right. Rational and irrational never overlap. The supposition led to something impossible, so it is false.

p.done.text: That is an indirect proof: suppose the opposite, follow it to something impossible, and conclude the opposite is false. Sam was wrong, and no digits need checking.
